content: Breastfeeding or providing breast milk to infants from a lactating woman infected with the Zika virus has implications for health equity. It is essential to evaluate the acceptability and feasibility of breastfeeding or feeding breast milk to infants in such cases. Additionally, it is critical to assess how modifications in infant feeding practices affect key infant health outcomes, particularly among those impacted by complications associated with Zika virus infection. This includes evaluating the resources, feasibility, acceptability, and equity of these modifications. Providing additional support and follow-up to caregivers to improve infant feeding practices can significantly impact infants affected by Zika virus-related complications. This requires an evaluation of the resources, feasibility, acceptability, continuity, and equity of such support systems. The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to monitor research developments in infant feeding in areas with Zika virus transmission. This includes tracking the availability of a Zika virus vaccine in the market. WHO employs a dynamic system to prioritize technical products, norms, standards, and research for country-level impact. It also maintains literature surveillance to respond rapidly to changes in Zika virus epidemiology and emerging evidence, ensuring that accurate, relevant, and up-to-date guidance is available globally. Zika virus is an arbovirus belonging to the Flavivirus genus. It was first identified in sentinel rhesus monkeys in Uganda's Zika forest in 1948 and later isolated from Aedes africanus mosquitoes in the same region. Sporadic cases of Zika virus infection were recorded in Africa and Asia between the 1960s and 1980s. The first outbreak occurred in 2007 on the Micronesian island of Yap, followed by larger outbreaks in French Polynesia in 2013 and Brazil in 2015, spreading to other countries in the Americas. By July 2019, 87 countries and territories in subtropical and tropical regions reported mosquito-transmitted Zika virus infections. In October 2019, the first locally acquired case was confirmed in France. Zika virus infection rates exhibit spatial heterogeneity, creating pockets of susceptible populations that could sustain future transmission. Symptoms in the general population are typically mild, resembling a flu-like febrile illness lasting a few days. However, the most concerning aspect of Zika virus infection is its impact during pregnancy, as it can cause microcephaly, congenital malformations, and fetal demise. Diagnosis involves serological tests for Zika virus antibodies (IgM or IgG) or nucleic acid amplification tests for viral RNA. These methods have limitations, including false-positive and false-negative results, and are only effective during a short window of viremia. Zika virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, particularly Aedes aegypti. It can also be transmitted through sexual contact, blood transfusion, blood products, or organ transplantation. The virus has been detected in various bodily fluids, including urine, saliva, amniotic fluid, genital secretions, semen, cerebrospinal fluid, and breast milk. Vertical transmission through transplacental passage or during birth has been documented. Concerns exist regarding the potential transmission of Zika virus during breastfeeding, as the virus has been detected in breast milk samples. However, it remains unclear whether breast milk contains sufficient viral load or infectivity to cause infection in infants or whether it possesses antiviral properties. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life and continued breastfeeding up to two years and beyond. An in vitro study demonstrated that human milk exhibits antiviral activity against Zika virus and Usutu virus at all stages of lactation. The mechanism involves hampering the binding of flaviviruses to cells rather than inactivating viral particles. During breastfeeding, other bodily fluids, such as sweat and blood, may also be exchanged. Transmission of Zika virus from mother to fetus during pregnancy can result in microcephaly and other congenital anomalies, collectively referred to as congenital Zika syndrome. Microcephaly can lead to seizures, hearing and vision deficits, intellectual disability, impaired development, and life-threatening complications. Zika virus infection may also cause Guillain-Barré syndrome, including acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, acute motor axonal neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia. Neurodevelopmental abnormalities, hearing and vision impairments, and other complications may manifest postnatally, primarily during the first year of life. Proper nutritional status is a significant concern for infants with congenital Zika syndrome. Poor nutrition may result from decreased muscle tone, reduced feeding, dysphagia, feeding difficulties, gastroesophageal reflux, delayed gastric emptying, and abnormal metabolic demands due to spasticity. Support for caregivers of affected infants is crucial for optimizing long-term nutritional status, achieving developmental milestones, and enhancing quality of life. This support may reduce the need for additional healthcare services in the future. Although the Zika virus outbreak has subsided, transmission continues in some regions. Standardized guidelines are essential for managing infant feeding in areas with ongoing transmission. WHO has updated its interim guidance on Zika virus, including recommendations for preventing sexual transmission. As new data on long-term outcomes of Zika virus infection in infants become available, WHO will update its guidelines on infant feeding in affected areas, following its established processes for guideline development.
